title: 160 Meter Band
snippet: Primarily a night-time band; heavy static in summer thunderstorm season. Voice activity mostly above 1.840–1.900 MHz.

title: 80/75 Meter Band
snippet: Good regional night-time HF band; popular for regional nets and ragchews.

title: 60 Meter Band (Channelized)
snippet: 4 channel centers: 5332.0, 5348.0, 5373.0, 5405.0 kHz, plus a reduced-power secondary WRC-15 segment at 5351.5–5366.5 kHz. Rules here changed as recently as December 2025 - reverify current rules before any transmit use.
freq: 5330.5–5406.4 kHz (4 fixed channels + a lower-power secondary segment)

title: 40 Meter Band
snippet: Reliable regional/continental night-time HF band; one of the most consistently active ham HF bands after dark.

title: 30 Meter Band
snippet: Narrow shared band; mostly CW and FT8/other digital activity, rarely voice.

title: 20 Meter Band
snippet: The most popular HF DX (long-distance) band; often active worldwide nearly any time of day.

title: 17 Meter Band
snippet: WARC band (no contests permitted); good daytime DX band.

title: 15 Meter Band
snippet: Daytime band, strongly tied to the solar/sunspot cycle - can be excellent or nearly dead depending on solar activity.

title: 12 Meter Band
snippet: WARC band; narrow, daytime, solar-cycle dependent.

title: 10 Meter Band
snippet: FM repeaters/simplex cluster near 29.520–29.680 MHz. Otherwise very solar-cycle dependent - can be nearly dead for years, then open worldwide during high solar activity.

title: 6 Meter Band
snippet: Nicknamed ‘the Magic Band’ - usually quiet, but sporadic-E and other propagation can unpredictably open it for long-distance contacts.

title: 2 Meter Band
snippet: The most popular VHF ham band. National FM simplex calling frequency: 146.520 MHz. FM repeater outputs are commonly found across 144–148 MHz per local band plan.

title: 1.25 Meter Band
snippet: Less common band - fewer radios support it. 222.100 MHz is a widely-used national simplex calling frequency in many regions.

title: 70 Centimeter Band
snippet: Second most popular ham VHF/UHF band after 2m. National FM simplex calling frequency: 446.000 MHz. Widely used for repeaters and digital voice (DMR/D-STAR/System Fusion).

title: AM Broadcast (Mediumwave)
snippet: AM travels far at night via skywave (ionospheric) propagation - distant stations often become audible after dark that are inaudible during the day.
freq: 535–1705 kHz (540–1700 kHz channelized, 10 kHz spacing, 117 channels)

title: FM Broadcast
snippet: Line-of-sight VHF propagation - range is mostly limited by antenna height/terrain, not time of day (unlike AM).

title: Shortwave Broadcast
snippet: Best reception varies a lot by band, time of day, and season - lower bands tend to favor night reception, higher bands favor daytime; all of it is sensitive to solar activity.

title: NOAA Weather Radio (All Hazards)
snippet: Continuous weather broadcast plus All Hazards alerts (severe weather and some non-weather emergencies). Typical range ~40 miles from a full-power transmitter over level terrain. Coverage depends on the specific transmitter serving your location, not just your state. Channel numbering (WX1–WX7) is a common radio-manufacturer convention, not an official NOAA designation - confirm by frequency, not channel number.

title: Citizens Band (CB) Radio
snippet: Normally short-range ground-wave propagation (a few miles), but can skip long distances during sporadic-E or other solar/atmospheric conditions.

title: FRS (Family Radio Service)
snippet: Real-world range is usually well under 1 mile in typical terrain, despite marketing claims of much longer range.

title: GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service)
snippet: Repeaters can extend usable range to roughly 20+ miles depending on antenna height/terrain. Per a 2024 FCC clarification, GMRS repeaters may not be linked to each other over the internet.
freq: 462.550–467.725 MHz (22 shared channels + repeater input pairs on ch.15-22)

title: MURS (Multi-Use Radio Service)
snippet: Generally less crowded than FRS/GMRS in many areas; popular for trail, farm, and property use.

title: Marine VHF
snippet: Channel 16 = international distress/calling/safety. Channel 9 = recreational hailing (alternate to 16 in many areas). Channel 13 = bridge-to-bridge navigation safety. Channel 22A/1022 = USCG safety/weather announcements. Channel 70 = digital calling only, no voice.

title: Aviation / Airband
snippet: Deliberately uses AM, not FM - lets a stronger nearby signal be heard over a weaker one instead of one completely blocking the other ('capture effect'), which matters for safety. Standard US channel spacing is 25 kHz (8.33 kHz in parts of Europe). HF (2.850–22 MHz, USB) is used for oceanic/remote-area voice beyond VHF range.

title: Railroad Radio
snippet: Uses an AAR-coordinated channel plan (roughly 97 channels, 15 kHz spacing) for dispatch, road/yard operations, and defect detectors. Specific channel-to-railroad/purpose assignments are regional and change over time - consult a current regional scanner/railfan frequency guide for your area rather than relying on a fixed list here.
freq: approximately 159.6–161.6 MHz (exact lower edge unconfirmed - see note)

title: AM (Amplitude Modulation)
snippet: Signal strength (amplitude) varies to carry sound. Simple and tolerant of weak-signal fading, and lets a stronger station be heard over a weaker one on the same frequency instead of blocking it outright.

title: FM / NFM (Narrowband Frequency Modulation)
snippet: Signal frequency varies slightly to carry sound. Used for most two-way land-mobile voice. Generally clearer than AM in strong-signal conditions, but the weaker of two same-frequency signals is usually blocked entirely (the 'capture effect') rather than heard faintly underneath.

title: WFM (Wideband FM)
snippet: Wide-deviation FM used for commercial FM broadcast - much higher audio fidelity than narrowband FM, but uses far more bandwidth. On a wideband receiver, WFM is usually a separate mode setting from (N)FM, not the same one.

title: USB (Upper Sideband)
snippet: A form of single-sideband voice (roughly half of an AM signal, more efficient for a given power). Used by amateur-radio convention above 10 MHz, plus HF airband and marine SSB. Sounds badly garbled if tuned even slightly off-frequency - fine adjustment matters.

title: LSB (Lower Sideband)
snippet: The other half of single-sideband voice - same technical concept as USB, just the other sideband. Used by amateur-radio convention on 160m/80m/60m/40m. The USB/LSB split by band is a long-standing operating custom, not a technical requirement.

title: CW (Continuous Wave / Morse Code)
snippet: The carrier is simply switched on and off to send Morse code - no voice. Extremely narrow bandwidth, so CW signals can often be copied through noise/interference where a voice signal couldn't.

title: What to Monitor During Severe Weather / an Emergency
snippet: Start with NOAA Weather Radio (162.400–162.550 MHz, NFM) for official forecasts and All Hazards alerts - it's the single most reliable receive-only source here.

snippet: A single steady tone switching on and off in short (dit) and long (dah) bursts - unmistakable once heard. Often sounds musical/rhythmic from a skilled operator.

title: Thunderstorms & Lightning
snippet: If you can hear thunder, you're close enough to be struck.

title: Tornadoes
snippet: Get to the lowest, most interior, windowless room you can, right away.

title: Flooding
snippet: Turn Around, Don't Drown - never walk, swim, or drive through flood water.

title: Earthquakes
snippet: Drop, Cover, and Hold On the moment you feel shaking.

title: Wildfire & Smoke
snippet: Evacuate immediately if told to; otherwise reduce smoke exposure indoors.

title: Extreme Heat
snippet: Recognize heat exhaustion vs. heat stroke - heat stroke is a 911 emergency.

title: Extreme Cold & Winter Weather
snippet: Hypothermia and frostbite both need warmth first - know the signs.

title: When the Power Goes Out
snippet: Keep freezers/fridges closed and have a plan for medical devices.

title: Downed Power Lines
snippet: Assume every downed line is live - stay back and call it in.

title: Generator Safety
snippet: Generators belong outside, far from windows - never in a garage or basement.

title: Carbon Monoxide Safety
snippet: CO is invisible and odorless - symptoms feel like the flu.

title: Alternative Lighting & Fire Safety
snippet: Use flashlights instead of candles during an outage.

title: Water Storage & Boil-Water Advisories
snippet: Store 1 gallon per person per day; follow local guidance on advisories.

title: Food Safety During an Outage
snippet: When in doubt, throw it out.

title: Sanitation Without Running Water
snippet: Plan for toilets before you need one - poor sanitation spreads disease fast.

title: Family Emergency Communication Plan
snippet: Pick an out-of-town contact - long-distance calls/texts often work when local ones don't.

title: Evacuation
snippet: If told to evacuate, go - don't wait to see how bad it gets.

title: Shelter-in-Place vs. Evacuating
snippet: Sometimes staying put is safer than trying to leave.

title: When Phones & Internet Are Down
snippet: Text over talk, and know your offline fallback.

title: Battery & Power Conservation
snippet: Assume you won't be able to recharge - make it last.

title: Pets in an Emergency
snippet: If it's not safe for you to stay, it's not safe for your pet either.

title: Get Professional Help - Check, Call, Care
snippet: Scene safety first, then call 911 for anything life-threatening.

title: CPR / AED Overview
snippet: For an unresponsive person not breathing normally: call 911, get an AED, and begin CPR if trained.

title: Choking (Conscious Adult/Child)
snippet: Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object clears.

title: Severe (Life-Threatening) Bleeding
snippet: Direct pressure first; a tourniquet if bleeding on a limb won't stop.

title: Shock
snippet: Pale, cool, clammy skin and a fast weak pulse are early warning signs.

title: Burns
snippet: Cool the burn under clean, cool running water for 10-20 minutes.

title: Minor Cuts & Wounds
snippet: Clean it, cover it, and watch for signs of infection.

title: Sprains & Fractures
snippet: Rest, immobilize, cool, and elevate - don't try to straighten a deformed limb.

title: Head Injury Warning Signs
snippet: Watch closely after any bump to the head - some warning signs appear later.

title: Seizures
snippet: Protect them from injury - don't restrain, and don't put anything in their mouth.

title: Poisoning
snippet: Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) or 911 - don't guess at home remedies.

title: Allergic Reaction / Anaphylaxis
snippet: Anaphylaxis can turn life-threatening within minutes - epinephrine, not antihistamines, is the treatment.

title: Heat Exhaustion & Heat Stroke
snippet: Heat stroke (hot, dry/red skin, confusion) is a 911 emergency - cool the person immediately.

title: Hypothermia & Frostbite
snippet: Warm the person gradually - never with direct high heat, and never rub frostbitten skin.

title: Insect Bites, Stings & Snake Bites
snippet: Watch for allergic reaction after any sting; call 911 immediately for any snake bite.

title: First-Aid Kit Reference
snippet: A basic kit covers most minor injuries and buys time for anything bigger.

title: Latitude & Longitude Basics
snippet: Latitude = how far north/south of the equator; longitude = how far east/west of the Prime Meridian.

title: Coordinate Formats (DD, DMS, UTM, MGRS)
snippet: The same location can be written several different ways - know which one your device/map uses.

title: How GPS Works Without Internet
snippet: GPS gets your position from satellites directly - it never needed the internet or cell service.

title: Cardinal Directions & Compass Bearings
snippet: N/E/S/W at 90° intervals; a bearing is the clockwise angle from north to your target.

title: Basic Offline Navigation Concepts
snippet: A paper map, a compass, and knowing your last confirmed position go a long way with zero electronics.

snippet: 911 - Universal in the US - not region-specific.
